City of Wonders

The start phase of our projected city has finally begun. The bickering architects and engineers have drafted plans that with the current estimate will take over a century to complete. By all accounts the city shall not be completed in a single generation, but in multiple.
By carefully investing in our capital, we can turn it into a magnificent Megalopolis that will outrival any other cities in the world. It shall become a City of Wonders.

[target_province.GetName] has been expanded into a proper city, but there still much to do. Many older buildings have been demolished to make room for many of the new districts that shall contain many of this city’s future wonders. Still, there is much to do, as you cannot even visit a single district without seeing it marred by construction work.

After much time and effort, [target_province.GetName] has turned into something everyone can agree is a Great City. Monuments and decorations have started to mark [target_province.GetName] as something extraordinary. Still, there is much to do, and the city requires quite a few more wonders before it can truly be called a City of Wonders.

[target_province.GetName] has undeniably become a Metropolis, that is quite possibly not just the center of the realm, but also a epicenter of the region it inhabits. It has by most margins become the most important post of every major trade route in the known world. Many districts have been built, and quite a few great works and monuments have raised. While the city is one of the greatest in the known world, there is still much work and renovations left before the city can reach it's apex.

[target_province.GetName] has incontestably grown into a fully-fledged Megalopolis, quite conceivably the greatest city ever built. Pedestrians can walk miles without seeing an apparent end to the city. In any district of the city you can find radiant wonders and great works never before seen beyond the city walls. It may have taken a few generations to accomplish this, and cost some blood, sweat, and wealth beyond imagining – but any who walks the beautifully paved streets of [target_province.GetName] agrees that any sacrifice would be worth it for such a magnificent city. It truly has become a City of Wonders!

The last bastion of the Freehold, the grand city of Volantis is the largest and most powerful of the Free Cities. Sprawling across the mouth of the Rhoyne, Old Volantis is a city of wonders. Built by the Valyrians, the Long Bridge across the Rhoyne is a structural masterpiece. It connects Old Volantis with the western part of the city. The massive Black Walls in the east are home to the proud descendants of the dragonlords. Outside the Walls is the magnificent Temple of the Lord of Light. Three times the size of the Great Sept of Baelor, it is the center of the Rhllor faith in Essos.

The bastard daughter of Valyria is the richest of all nine of the Free Cities, even more than Volantis. The tall Titan of Braavos welcomes ships that enter the lagoon, with a sword held up high. At the center of Braavos is the Isle of the Gods, a node of religious activity. The Temple of the Moonsingers is the largest on the isle. Its beautiful architecture features an exquisite white marble and silver dome. Close by is the infamous House of Black and White, home of the Faceless Men & a place of worship for the Many-Faced God.

The city of Qarth, situated on the Jade Gates, controls the entrance to the Far East and beyond. The Queen of Cities is home to the famous Triple Wall, an architectural masterpiece and wonder of man. Engraved into the Triple Wall are scenes of war, fauna, and love. The city inside is no less splendid. The most famous sites are the Hall of a Thousand Thrones, the palace of Xaro Xhoan Daxos, and the House of the Undying.

Meereen

This bastion of the ancient Ghiscari Empire is the most powerful of the Slaver Cities. The Ghiscari nobles governing Meereen are the Great Masters. They rule from grand pyramids dotted throughout the city. The most wondrous of these is the Great Pyramid, built to echo the now ruined Great Pyramid of Old Ghis. Golden domes lie atop the magnificent Temple of the Graces. Meanwhile, many fighting pits dot the grand city--including the Great Pit of Daznak.

The Wise Masters rule the grand city of Yunkai with an iron hold. This Slaver City is home to the Golden Pyramid of Qaggaz, the largest of Yunkai's pyramids. More disreputable than Meereen, Yunkai's Wise Masters are cunning but tainted by corruption.

Called the Red City, Astapor is the southernmost of the Slaver Cities and closest to the ruins of Old Ghis. Like her northern sister Meereen, fighting pits dot the entirety of Astapor. Most famous are the Unsullied, trained from birth to become formidable war machines. “Bricks and blood built Astapor, and bricks and blood her people.”

The great city of Oldtown is the most prosperous in Westeros. This city of wonders sprawls around the Hightower, home to the legendary house of the same name. Oldtown's massive harbor, at the mouth of the Honeywine, features galleys from the Jade Gates and beyond. More famous is the Citadel, the center of the order of maesters in Westeros. Here, the archmaesters train new students and do their mysterious studies. Further splendid is Starry Sept, once the center of the Faith of the Seven. Its black marble walls soar into the sky as if reaching out to the Seven themselves.

King’s Landing

A group of hills only three centuries ago, the seat of the Iron Throne has become the most populous city in the realm. On Aegon’s High Hill, the Red Keep stands at the mouth of the Blackwater Rush. Built by Maegor the Cruel, the seven red drum-towers overlook the city, behind high red walls. Within the Red Keep are the Iron Throne, Tower of the Hand, Maidenvault, and the infamous black cells. Underground passages seem to twist and turn underneath the keep. West of the Red Keep is Visenya's Hill, on which sits the Great Sept of Baelor. The grand home of the High Septon, the Great Sept's only rival is the Starry Sept in Oldtown. To the south, past the slums of Flea Bottom, is Rhaenys' Hill. There, the dilapidated ruin of the Dragonpit lies with its broken bronze dome.

The great city of Yin is the largest of the YiTish ports on the Jade Sea and a nexus for many of the trade routes in eastern Essos. The grey, indigo, pearl-white, and the azure God-Emperors have used Yin as their capital. Corlys Velaryon returned from Yin with silk, spice, and jade. It was enough to make House Velaryon the wealthiest house in Westeros.

The Shadow Council has ruled the Port of Ibben since the Doom of Valyria. The Thousand, a large assembly of Ibbish noblemen, elect the Shadow Council. The port is the largest settlement on the bleak isle of Ib. Its most notable structure is the colossal palace of the God-Kings of old. The ruined castle, though, has been barren since the Doom, when the Ibbish overthrew the last God-King.

A remnant of the Freehold, Elyria was mostly unaffected by the Doom. It continues to be one of the wealthiest and prominent cities on Slaver’s Bay. Now, it shares closer ties to the Slaver Cities to the east. The nobility of Ghiscari descent governs the island city.

The legendary city of Asshai-by-the-Shadow sits at the eastern end of the Jade Sea & the edge of the known world. Its shadowbinders practice some of the most advanced sorcery in the world. The people of Asshai are mysterious and hold an ominous reputation. Asshai's great black wall is so large that it could contain Volantis, Qarth, King’s Landing, and Oldtown. Gold, amber, and dragonglass are abundant in the gloomy city. Thus, they are the largest exports of its massive port, which is only rivaled by Yin. The same black stone of Asshai's walls makes up its buildings, giving the city its aura of evil and dread. Upriver on the River Ash are the terrible ruins of the city of corpses, Stygai. Horrifying monsters haunt Stygai, and even the shadowbinders fear to go there.

A dreadful, ruined island, the Isle of Tears is the largest of the Basilisk Isles north of Sothoryos. Once a Ghiscari colony called Gogai, the Valyrians conquered it in the Third Ghiscari War. The dragonlords renamed it to Gogossos and used it as a massive slave colony. After the Doom, it grew powerful in the Century of Blood--it continued to be a nexus of the slave trade in Essos. However, the Red Death decimated the populations of Gogossos and the surrounding islands. To this day, the Isle of Tears is mostly uninhabited.

Five thousand years ago, the ruins of Old Ghis once served as the capital of the vast Ghiscari Empire. The legendary Grazdan the Great founded the great city. He would go on to conquer Slaver's Bay with his formidable lockstep legions. Colossal ruins of ancient pyramids straddle Old Ghis. The largest is the Great Pyramid of Old Ghis, far grander than the Great Pyramid of Meereen to the north. The city fell, though, after the Fifth Ghiscari War when the Valyrians razed Old Ghis to the ground.

Pentos is the westernmost of the Free Cities, the daughters of Old Valyria. Since the Doom, a council of magisters and the Prince of Pentos have ruled the Free City. In Pentos, wealth is power. The Pentoshi nobility and wealthy merchants own massive walled estates nearby the port. Meanwhile, Pentoshi spice traders live in square brick towers. Though it has high walls surrounding it, Pentos is still the most vulnerable of the Free Cities. A large red temple serves the majority Rhllor population.

Qohor is the easternmost of the Free Cities. The dark arts run rampant within its stone walls. Among these arts are divination, blood magic, and even necromancy. Worshipped is the Black Goat, a dark god as dark as Qohorik sorcery. The city lies on the western terminus of overland trade routes stretching from as far as Asshai. Qohor's location and the valuables in the Forest of Qohor provide an enormity of wealth. Qohor is famous for its forges, which make stunning metalwork far superior to that of Westeros. Qohorik forges guard the close-kept secret to reforging Valyrian steel.

Though it is the poorest of the Free Cities, the city of Lorath is rich in its heritage. Many groups have left their imprint on Lorath. The ancient mazemakers built grandiose mazes sprawling across the Lorathi isles. Now, though, they are ruins. The Andals later colonized the islands, until Valyrians razed Lorath during the Scouring. Afterward, the cult of Boash, or the Blind God, built large temples where the mazes once were. Since the extinction of the Boash, though, a council of magisters rules Lorath. The city is famous for its beautiful purple velvets, but fishing remains its source of wealth. Lorath has a massive fleet of fishing vessels. It provides an abundance of cod, walrus tusks, sealskins, and whale oil for export.

Norvos lies on the intersection of the Noyne and an ancient Valyrian road used by caravans from the Far East. Norvos is most famous for its Three Bells, said by Lomas Longstrider himself to be a wonder of the world. Noom, Narrah, and Nyel govern every aspect of Norvosi life. Divided into two parts, Norvos has a high city and a low city. The high city, where nobility dwell, is atop a high hill and surrounded by high stone walls. Most notable is the mighty fortress-temple of the Bearded Priests. The lower city, on the banks of the Noyne, is where most Norvosi live. Astone stair called the Sinner’s Steps connects both the high and lower city.

The wealthy Free City of Myr is the most advanced of her sisters, with her brilliance in the arts and learning. Renowned Myrish artisans churn out high-quality finished goods. These include their lenses, tapestries, nectar wine, Myrish lace, and Myrish fire. The city is on a point where an ancient Valyrian road meets the Sea of Myrth. Many different temples are within Myr, especially the red temples of Rhllor. The Myrish are a seafaring folk, and their large port feeds the Narrow Sea trade.

The Valyrian dragonlords first settled Lys as a paradise resort, and it continues to be so. Sellswords defend the walled city, and a conclave of wealthy magisters rule it. Its pleasure gardens and pillow houses are famous throughout the world. The blood of Old Valyria runs strong in Lys. Even the smallfolk share the silver hair & purple eyes of the Valyrian dragonlords. Many buildings of faith are in the city, including the Temple of Trade, Temple of Yndros, and some red temples. Slavery is crucial to the Lyseni economy. Lyseni pillow houses utilize eugenics to breed the most beautiful slaves. The infamous Lyseni alchemists make many poisons--including the tears of Lys and strangler.

Tyroshi artisans produce fine metalwork and most brutal torture devices. Within Tyrosh's inner walls of black dragonstone are many houses of faith. Most famous is the Temple of Trios, with a fearsome three-headed dog guarding its entrance.

A city of ruins, Ny Sar is at the confluence of the Rhoyne and its tributary, the Noyne. The last princess of Ny Sar, Nymeria, abandoned it after the defeat of Garin the Great. Eventually, she would make her way to Dorne. Her massive palace of pink and green marble is the most notable of Ny Sar's ruins. Horned turtles swim along the banks of the confluence.

The ruins of Sarnath’s ancient capital, Sarnath of the Tall Towers, lay to rest in Vaes Kweho. Once the greatest of the Tall Men cities in the Kingdom of Sarnath, it fell after the Dothraki put it to the torch. The mythical Palace of a Thousand Rooms, where the High King of Sarnath once ruled from, is now rubble. Lomas Longstrider, the famous adventurer, called it one of the nine wonders of man.

That was until both fell to the Dothraki in the Century of Blood. Now, Essaria lies in ruins called by the Dothraki as Vaes Khadokh.

Temple of the Lord of Light

Third Temple

With The Third Temple built, all Jews can finally rejoice with the sacred knowledge that the Temple stands once again upon the Temple Mount in the Holy City of Jerusalem. Great Temple

Pantheum of Roma

The Pantheon was built between AD 113–125 during Hadrian's reign at the site of an earlier temple commissioned by Marcus Agrippa during Augustus' reign (27 BC – AD 14). In 609, the Byzantine emperor Phocas gave the building to Pope Boniface IV, who converted it into a Christian church and consecrated it to St. Mary and the Martyrs. This sacrilegious conversion has finally been revoked, and once again do Hellenic priests dwell inside the Pantheon in the name of [Root.Religion.GetHighGodNameCap].
Serapeion of Alexandreia

The Serapeum of Alexandria has been rebuilt, and is once again a place of devotion and reflection. The Serapeum was originally an ancient Greek temple built by Ptolemy III Euergetes which was dedicated to Serapis, who was made the protector of Alexandria.
Parthenon of Athenai

The Parthenon is once again a temple dedicated to the Goddess of Wisdom, Athena. All the sacrilegious alterations committed by the misguided Christians have been removed, and the Temple has been completely cleansed of their influence.
Temple of the Yi Ti gods

Konark Sun Temple

It is the primary line of defense for Braavos. The Titan is one of the nine Wonders Made by Man in the book written by Lomas Longstrider.

Great Walls

Teichos Theodosiakon
The Theodosian Walls were built during the reign of Emperor Theodosius II in the early 5th century, but they still remain some of the most formidable fortifications built by human hands.
Murus Aurelianus

The Aurelian Walls were built during the reign of Emperor Aurelian and Probus late in the 3rd century, but they still remain the most formidable fortifications ever built in Roma. With a few overhauls, the Aurelian Walls have become as impregnable as the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople!
Makra Teiche

The Long Walls of Athens were once a vital set of walls that connects Athens to its ports at Piraeus and Phaleron. The walls were destroyed by the Roman general Sulla after his Siege of Athens and Piraeus in 87-86 BC. With the Long Walls rebuilt, once again has Athens secured itself crucial access to the sea.
Nimitti-Bel

The Walls of Babylon were a set of impenetrable walls that completely encircled the city of Babylon. The only way to enter the city was through either one of the many city gates or the Euphrates river. Metal grates were installed underwater, allowing the river to flow through the city walls while preventing intrusion. When presented with the challenge of sieging Babylon, Cyrus the Great of Persia devised a ingenious plan. By diverting the Euphrates River upstream, the Persians lowered the water level enough so that they could enter the city via the river.\n\nWith the new Grand Walls being greatly inspired from these ancient walls, the architects took great measures to ensure that Cyrus' stunt can not be repeated with the Tigris River.
City of Peace
The City of Peace, more commonly known as the Round City of Baghdad is the core of Baghdad. By expanding the city with a set of near impregnable defensive walls, Baghdad shall never be defiled.

Magnificent Garden

Phoros Konstantinou

The Forum of Constantine was built at the foundation of Constantinople immediately outside the old city walls of Byzantium. It marked the centre of the new city, and was a central point along the Mese, the main ceremonial road through the city. It was circular and had two monumental gates to the east and west. The Column of Constantine, which was crowned with Constantine as Apollo, was erected in the centre of the square.
Forum Romanum

The Roman Forum is a rectangular forum (plaza) surrounded by several important ancient government buildings at the center of the city of Rome. Citizens of the ancient city referred to this space, originally a marketplace, as the Forum Magnum, or simply the Forum. For centuries the Forum was the center of day-to-day life in Rome: the site of triumphal processions and elections - the venue for public speeches, criminal trials, and gladiatorial matches - and the nucleus of commercial affairs. Here statues and monuments commemorated the city's great men. The teeming heart of ancient Rome, it has been called the most celebrated meeting place in the world, and in all history. Refurbished it shall once again become the center of a great realm.
Hanging Gardens of Babylon

The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were once one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World according to the Hellenes. It was described as a remarkable feat of engineering with an ascending series of tiered gardens containing a wide variety of trees, shrubs, and vines, resembling a large green mountain constructed of mud bricks. With the Hanging Gardens built anew, no longer can anyone question the grandiose and heritage of our great city.

The Circus Maximus (Latin for greatest or largest circus) is an ancient Roman chariot-racing stadium and mass entertainment venue located in Roma. Situated in the valley between the Aventine and Palatine Hills, it was the first and largest stadium in ancient Rome and its later Empire. It measured 621 m (2,037 ft) in length and 118 m (387 ft) in width and could accommodate over 150,000 spectators. In its fully developed form, it became the model for circuses throughout the Roman Empire.
